title: One Platform, 20+ Manufacturing Facilities: How GM Standardized on the Stratasys F900 Across a Global Network
summary: Discover how GM standardized on the Stratasys F900 across 20+ facilities to share tooling designs, print spare parts locally and scale additive manufacturing.
body_markdown:
### Why the F900 for standardization?


The F900's broad material compatibility, spanning commodity thermoplastics to high-performance polymers like ULTEM™ 1010 resin and Nylon 12CF, means a single platform can address every application class: ergonomic hand tools in ABS, UV-stable exterior fixtures in ASA, high-stiffness structural jigs in carbon-fiber-filled nylon, and heat-resistant tooling in ULTEM™. That versatility is what makes true network-wide standardization possible.


### **From reactive to proactive**


The standardization strategy has shifted GM's manufacturing engineering mindset. When new equipment is being designed for plants, engineers now factor in the distributed Stratasys FDM network from the start.


Odegaard says; "When we design equipment going into plants, we know we've got the distributed network. And now we can challenge our suppliers to look at additive so that we can look at our spare parts inventory."


The implications are significant: GM is digitizing its spare parts inventory, reducing the complexity and cost of maintaining physical stock across dozens of facilities. If a part breaks, the digital file is already in the system. Print it locally on the F900, install it the same day.
